label: The epitaph of Abercius, a bishop, attests organized Christianity at Hieropolis in Phrygia

place.note: Ramsay identified Abercius' see as Hieropolis in the Sandikli valley (Phrygian Pentapolis), mod. Kochisar (Pleiades 609403), from the find-spot of the inscription fragments at nearby Kelendres. This is not Hierapolis ad Lycum / Pamukkale (638860), the Lycus-valley city attested from Colossians (lit-colossians-hierapolis). The identification is probable, not certain: the medieval Life of Abercius and some older scholarship attach him instead to the better-known Hierapolis.

date.note: Abercius flourished under Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161-180) and composed the epitaph at the age of 72. Terminus ante quem 216: the epitaph of Alexander, dated 216, quotes it. The consensus places the Abercius inscription at the end of the 2nd century.

primary.cite: Epitaph of Abercius (the Abercius inscription); stone fragments and the fuller text preserved in the Life of Abercius

secondary.cite: Harnack, Mission and Expansion, vol. 2, p. 188; synopsis at p. 95
W. M. Ramsay, discovery and identification of the Abercius inscription (fragments found 1882-83 at Kelendres / Hieropolis)

notes: Harnack (p. 188): 'however one may view the famous inscription of Abercius, we may infer from it that Christianity had by that time reached Hieropolis.' The epitaph, in symbolic language, names a shepherd-taught traveller who went to Rome and beyond the Euphrates and everywhere found the faith setting bread and mixed cup before him; it is the oldest inscription to mention the Eucharist. The stone fragments Ramsay recovered are in the Vatican, Museo Pio Cristiano.
